etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English handel, handle, from Old English handle (“a handle”), from handlian (“to handle, feel, deal with, discuss”). See verb below. Cognate with Danish handel (“a handle”).

definitions.definition: The part of an object which is (designed to be) held in the hand when used or moved.

quote.citation: 1854, John Hovey Robinson, Silver-knife: or, The hunters of the Rocky Mountains‎[1], page 133:
quote.text: Once his fingers strayed to the handle of his hunting-knife, and I should have interfered had I not been conscious that Wickliffe was on his guard.

quote.citation: 1902, “Atomic Weight of Lanthanum”, in Journal of the Chemical Society‎[2], volume 81, part 2:
quote.text: By pushing the fork downwards so that its teeth pass the handle of the stopper, and then turning the cover of the desiccator 90°, the handle of the stopper falls into the furrows and rests upon them.

quote.citation: 1905, “Origin of the Respiratory Sounds”, in Proceedings of the Royal Society of London‎[3], volume 37:
quote.text: By keeping the handle of the bellows fixed in any given position the lung within the chamber could be kept for a short time at any desired degree of distension, and by pressing at intervals upon the bag, air could be forced to and fro between the bad and the lung outside the chamber, without distending the air within it.

quote.citation: 1972, Frank Zappa (lyrics and music), “Billy the Mountain”:
quote.text: But first they were gonna stop in Las Vegas / It's off to Las Vegas / To check out the lounges / Pull a few handles

definitions.definition: An instrument for effecting a purpose (either literally or figuratively); a tool, or an opportunity or pretext.

quote.citation: 1692–1717, Robert South, Twelve Sermons Preached upon Several Occasions, volume (please specify |volume=I to VI), London:
quote.text: They overturned him to all his interests by the sure but fatal handle of his own good nature.

quote.citation: 1894, Robert Needham Cust, Essay on the prevailing methods of the evangelization of the non-Christian world‎[4], page 70:
quote.text: Nothing can be more reprehensible, or wicked, than to make Christian Missions a handle for political expansion.

quote.citation: 1978, William Hay Taliaferro, John Herbert Humphrey, Advances in immunology‎[5], page 224:
quote.text: Many investigators feel that the double requirement for the antigen-recognition by cytotoxic T cells or DTH-reactive T cells may provide a handle for solving the T-cell receptor puzzle, and that anti-Id reagents are to be used in this approach.

quote.citation: 1985 December 28, Nancy Wechsler, “Boston Forum Calls for Radical Confrontation”, in Gay Community News, volume 13, number 24, page 2:
quote.text: The way AIDS has become a handle for the New Right's homophobia.

quote.citation: 1997, Allen S. Johnson, A prologue to revolution: the political career of George Grenville‎[6], →ISBN, page 95:
quote.text: Indeed, at the beginning of the session he was careful to make "no declarations of what might hereafter be measures, so as to give anybody a handle for fixing him down to any particular system."

definitions.definition: (gambling) The gross amount of wagering within a given period of time or for a given event at one of more establishments.

quote.citation: 2001, William Norman Thompson, Gambling in America: an encyclopedia of history, issues, and society‎[7], →ISBN, page 421:
quote.text: For a casino table game,the handle is difficult to determine, as it consists of all the bets made in every game, whether by chip or by cash play.

quote.citation: 2001, Harold L. Vogel, Travel industry economics: a guide for financial analysis‎[8], →ISBN, page 139:
quote.text: Note here, however, that the casino's "edge" (its expected value per unit bet, or, in casino jargon, the house p.c.) in table games is expressed as a percentage of the handle and not as a percentage of the drop (even though these might sometimes be the same).

quote.citation: 2007, Douglas M. Walker, The economics of casino gambling‎[9], →ISBN, page 77:
quote.text: The results for the dog racing model indicate that increases in lottery sales and decreases in horse racing handle and casino revenues in the state in question statistically increase dog racing handle.

definitions.definition: (textiles) The tactile qualities of a fabric, e.g., softness, firmness, elasticity, fineness, resilience, and other qualities perceived by touch.
(slang) A name or nickname, especially as an identifier over the radio or Internet.

quote.citation: 1997, Jack Canfield, Hanoch McCarty, A 4th course of chicken soup for the soul‎[10], →ISBN, page 312:
quote.text: We sat together at the restaurant and asked him about his handle (CB name).

quote.citation: 2001, Stephen King, Peter Straub, The Talisman‎[11], →ISBN:
quote.text: This was so unexpected that Jack came close to gabbling out his real name instead of the one he had used at the Golden Spoon, the name he also used if the people who picked him up asked for his handle.

quote.citation: 2007, Jon Evans, Invisible Armies‎[12], →ISBN, page 253:
quote.text: "I don't actually know his birth name. He just uses his handle."

definitions.definition: (slang) A title attached to one's name, such as Doctor or Colonel.
(computing) A reference to an object or structure that can be stored in a variable.

quote.citation: 1989, Petrus Maria Gerardus Apers, Gio Wiederhold, Proceedings of the Fifteenth International Conference on Very Large Data‎[13], page 383:
quote.text: A handle for a type instance is similar to an open file descriptor; it is used to reference that type instance when performing operations on it.

quote.citation: 2008, Stephen J. Chapman, MATLAB programming for engineers‎[14], →ISBN, page 354:
quote.text: By contrast, when a host function creates a handle for a nested function and returns that handle to a calling program, the host function's workspace is created and remains in existence for as long as the function handle remains in existence.

definitions.definition: (UK, informal) A traditional dimpled glass with a handle, for serving a pint of beer.
(Australia, chiefly Northern Territory, New Zealand) A 10 fluid ounce (285 mL) glass of beer.

quote.citation: 2002, Kate Duignan, Breakwater‎[15], Victoria University Press, →ISBN, page 86:

quote.citation: 2006, Rod Hylands, Lateral Connection‎[16], →ISBN, page 68:

quote.text: When ordering a beer, you'll get either a handle (mug) or a one-liter jug (pitcher).

definitions.definition: (US) A half-gallon (1.75-liter) bottle of alcohol.

definitions.definition: (geography, Newfoundland and Labrador, rare) A point, an extremity of land.
(topology) A topological space homeomorphic to a ball but viewed as a product of two lower-dimensional balls.

quote.citation: 2003, Gordana Matić, Clint McCrory, Topology and geometry of manifolds‎[18], →ISBN, page 182:
quote.text: Such a 2-handle cancels the 1-handle so the manifold is D4.

definitions.definition: (algebraic geometry) The smooth, irreducible subcurve of a comb which connects to each of the other components in exactly one point.
(slang) A person's nose.

quote.citation: 1811, Charles Lamb, Prince Dorus:
quote.text: That Nose, which in the infant could annoy, / Was grown a perfect nuisance in the boy. / Whene'er he walk'd, his Handle went before, / Long as the snout of Ferret, or Wild Boar;  […]

definitions.definition: (horse racing, gambling) The amount wagered in the various pari-mutuel pools for a particular event or events.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English handlen, from Old English handlian (“to handle, feel, deal with, discuss”), from Proto-West Germanic *handulōn, from Proto-Germanic *handulōną (“to take, grip, feel”), equivalent to hand +‎ -le. Cognate with West Frisian handelje, hanneljen, hanljen (“to handle, treat”), Dutch handelen (“to handle, deal, act, negotiate”), German handeln (“to act, trade, negotiate, behave”), Swedish handla (“to buy, trade, deal”), Icelandic höndla (“to handle”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To touch; to feel or hold with the hand(s).

definitions.definition: (transitive, rare) To accustom to the hand; to take care of with the hands.

quote.citation: 1679, William Temple, An essay upon the advancement of trade in Ireland.:
quote.text: The hardness of the winters forces the breeders to house and handle their colts for at least six months every year.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To manage, use, or wield with the hands.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1606, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of King Lear”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene vi]:

definitions.definition: (transitive) To manage, control, or direct.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “Measure for Measure”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:

quote.citation: 2011 December 16, Denis Campbell, “Hospital staff 'lack skills to cope with dementia patients'”, in Guardian‎[20]:
quote.text: The findings emerged from questionnaires filled in by 2,211 staff in 145 wards of 55 hospitals in England and Wales and 105 observations of care of dementia patients. Two-thirds of staff said they had not had enough training to provide proper care, 50% said they had not been trained how to communicate properly with such patients and 54% had not been told how to handle challenging or aggressive behaviour.
